passages.where: After his poem of a time for everything, the Teacher says God has made everything beautiful in its time and has set eternity in the human heart, yet people cannot grasp the whole of God's work. The site's note on the chapter sets this beside the fourteen pairs of opposites that fill a life. The heart carries a longing that no single season of life can fill.

The Teacher tests pleasure, wine and great projects, denying himself nothing his eyes desired, and when he looks at all he has done he finds it futile, a pursuit of the wind. The site's note says he ends the chapter recognizing that the simple ability to eat, drink and enjoy work comes from the hand of God. Getting everything did not settle him; receiving it from God was a different thing.

God calls everyone who is thirsty and has no money to come and eat for free, and asks why people spend their money on what is not bread and their labor on what does not satisfy. The site's note on the chapter says he offers an everlasting covenant and freely pardons those who return. The question is asked by the one who can actually feed them.

At Jacob's well Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that whoever drinks that water will thirst again, but the water he gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. The site's plain note says she wanted water so she would not have to keep walking to the well, and that he does not mock the smaller request but keeps offering more than was asked: himself.

In the dry wilderness of Judah, David says his soul thirsts for God and his body yearns for him in a weary land without water. The site's plain note says thirst is a sign of life, and that longing toward God is itself a kind of prayer. It notices that he is still in the desert when he says his soul is satisfied.

The LORD says his people have committed two evils: they have forsaken him, the fountain of living water, and dug their own cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water. The site's note on the chapter says they traded him for worthless idols and ran after foreign powers for help. Much restless searching is digging, again and again, where water will not stay.

The letter says a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters God's rest rests from his own work, as God did. The site's note says the rest is received by faith and yet calls for effort, a paradox the author leaves standing. The plain note asks whether a person lives as one who has entered God's rest, or as one still trying to prove themselves.

Writing from prison, Paul says he has learned to be content in any circumstance, in being filled and being hungry, in plenty and in need. The site's plain note says the strength Christ gave him was the strength to be content. Contentment, in his own word, was learned.

To a people rushing to Egypt for help, the LORD says that by repentance and rest they would be saved and their strength would lie in quiet confidence, but they were not willing. The site's note says the plan was made without asking his advice and rested their security on a foreign power. The chapter goes on to say the LORD longs to be gracious to them.

The people of faith confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth, longing for a better country, and God was not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. The site's plain note says being strangers does not mean not caring about the places we live: Abraham dug wells and made peace with his neighbours. Some longing is for a home that is not finished yet.

misread.taken: There is no peace for the wicked is said of anyone who cannot settle, or quoted at a restless believer as if not being able to rest proved something was wrong with their soul.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says it is about Judah's idolatry, and that the same chapter has the high and holy God dwelling with the contrite and lowly and promising healing and peace to those far and near, while the wicked remain like a restless sea. The restlessness it names belongs to those who will not turn to God, and the chapter's answer is a promise to anyone who does. It is not a verdict on a person who cannot sit still or sleep.

whole: Restlessness takes many shapes. Changing jobs every couple of years, scrolling late into the night, starting projects and dropping them, needing the next trip or purchase to look forward to, never able to sit in a quiet room. Sometimes it is a vague sense that real life is happening somewhere else. Sometimes it follows a success: the thing a person worked for arrives, and within a week it no longer satisfies. Restlessness of the body that will not let a person sleep or sit still can also be a sign of anxiety or of an illness, and it is worth telling a doctor about.

Scripture treats much restlessness as a true signal aimed at the wrong things. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes denied himself nothing his eyes desired, and when he looked at all he had done he called it a pursuit of the wind. He also says God has set eternity in the human heart, so that nothing within time can fill it. Jeremiah's picture for the same thing is digging cisterns: God's people left the fountain of living water and dug broken tanks that could not hold it. Isaiah asks why people spend their money on what is not bread and their labor on what does not satisfy. We are restless partly because we were made for more than anything we can get, and partly because we keep trying to get it from things that cannot give it. Scripture is honest that God's own people did this, and most of us will recognize ourselves.

So the Bible's wisdom is not to kill the longing but to take it to the right place. Jesus offered the woman at the well water that would become a spring within her, and Isaiah's invitation is to come without money and eat what is good. Paul says he learned to be content in plenty and in need; it was something he learned, not something he was born with. Isaiah told a people rushing to Egypt that their strength would lie in repentance and rest, in quiet confidence, and that they were not willing. It helps to notice what we reach for when we are restless and to bring the ache itself to God, as David did in the wilderness. And it helps to keep a rhythm of rest and worship, since the letter to the Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.

The hope Scripture gives is a homeland. The people of faith in Hebrews called themselves strangers and exiles, longing for a better country, and God was not ashamed to be called their God. Some restlessness will not be cured in this life, because it is a longing for a city that is not finished yet. That is no reason to despise the place you are in; Abraham dug wells and made peace with his neighbours. It is a reason to hold everything else more loosely, and to rest now in the one who has prepared that city.
sit: What do you reach for when you feel restless, and what would it mean to bring the restlessness itself to God before you reach?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says this psalm asks you to practise setting the LORD always before you, on purpose, as a daily habit. Pray it when you wake, before your mind turns anywhere else.
